Informed Consent: The Ritual That Replaced the Relationship

If the IRB system is an obstacle, the informed consent apparatus has become a cathedral — an enormous, ornate structure built to honor a principle that has been hollowed out from within.

The principle is sound. Human beings asked to participate in research must understand what they are agreeing to. Their participation must be voluntary. Their dignity must be respected. No serious person disputes any of this.

But the practice of informed consent as it currently exists in pharmaceutical research represents a grotesque distortion of this principle, one that serves the interests of institutional lawyers and regulatory compliance officers far more than it serves either patients or science.

The modern informed consent document for a Phase I oncology trial routinely runs anywhere from twelve to over thirty pages. It is written in a legalistic idiom that, by design, avoids clarity. It is peppered with arcane procedural language, vague risk enumerations, and boilerplate provisions addressing scenarios that bear little relationship to the actual trial under consideration. Patients — often desperately ill, often frightened, often confronting their own mortality for the first time — are handed this document and asked to sign it, frequently in the same appointment at which they receive their diagnosis. The result is not informed consent. It is institutional absolution masquerading as patient empowerment.

Research on patient comprehension of consent documents has produced findings that should shame the entire enterprise. Studies consistently demonstrate that even highly educated patients retain only a fraction of the information contained in these protracted forms, and the length and complexity of consent documents have been repeatedly shown to impede understanding rather than enhance it. Patients frequently confuse the research purpose of the trial with therapeutic intent, a misunderstanding that the lengthiest consent form in the world cannot remedy. Rather than bridging the knowledge gap, the current consent process deepens it by fostering an illusion of information transfer where none has occurred.

The ritual of informed consent also imposes a powerful chilling effect on the willingness of patients to participate in research. Surveys consistently reveal that the prospect of engaging with the consent process is a major deterrent for prospective research subjects, particularly among lower-income individuals and those with lower levels of formal education — populations that are already underrepresented in clinical trials and whose exclusion from research further compounds health inequities. The attempt to protect patients has become a mechanism for excluding them.

Moreover, the informed consent process as currently practiced fundamentally mischaracterizes the relationship between physician and patient. It presumes a model of autonomous, rational decision-making divorced from context, emotion, trust, and the overwhelming psychological burden of serious illness. It imagines the patient as a legal agent negotiating a contract, when what the patient actually is — in virtually every case — is a vulnerable human being placing their trust in a physician's judgment and in the broader scientific enterprise. The most ethical and most genuinely protective framework for human research is not a contractual model but a fiduciary one, grounded in the physician's duty of care, reinforced by professional ethics, and supported by robust mechanisms for scientific transparency and data sharing.

In place of the current consent regime, we should advocate for something radically simpler and more honest. For research posing no more than the kind of risks that patients routinely accept in the course of clinical care — which describes the vast majority of pharmaceutical trials conducted today — a streamlined consent process focused on the essential elements that patients most want to know should suffice. What is the purpose of this trial? What will participation involve? What are the main risks? What alternatives do I have? What will happen to my data? These questions can be — and should be — answered conversationally, in plain language, with the opportunity for extended dialogue with a trusted clinician and the involvement of family or other support persons as the patient desires. The signed document — where one is deemed necessary at all — should be brief, plain-spoken, and focused on genuine comprehension rather than legal defensibility.

To those who object that even these streamlined protections are essential to maintaining public trust in research, we must ask: trust built on what? On a lie? The current consent process does not build genuine trust — it builds the appearance of trust while systematically neglecting the conditions that would produce the real thing: transparency, honest communication, accountability for outcomes, and a demonstrated commitment to the welfare of research participants measured not by the thickness of their consent folder but by the quality of their care.

The Precautionary Principle Run Amok

Underpinning the continued expansion of pharmaceutical regulation is the precautionary principle, a philosophy that has hardened into dogma over recent decades despite the extraordinary cost it imposes on human welfare. In its most aggressive formulation, the precautionary principle holds that an activity should be restricted or prohibited until it can be demonstrated to be safe — that the burden of proof falls upon the proponent of change rather than the proponent of restraint.

This superficially appealing philosophy conceals a devastating logical error: it considers only the harms of action and ignores the harms of inaction. Every day that a promising therapy remains unavailable to patients because of regulatory caution is a day of preventable suffering. The precautionary principle, rigorously applied, would weigh these days of suffering and count them. It refuses to do so.

The result is a regulatory system with a built-in asymmetry: the harms it prevents are vivid, immediate, and attributable — a patient harmed in a clinical trial will generate headlines, litigation, and political accountability. The harms it causes are diffuse, delayed, and statistical — the patients who died from disease while a therapy sat in regulatory limbo leave no identifiable trace in any database. They do not appear in any adverse event report. They do not generate any congressional hearing. They simply die, often from the very conditions under which any reasonable risk-benefit calculus would have favored their participation in a trial. The regulatory system is meticulously accountable for the harms of commission and systematically blind to the harms of omission.

This is not a minor philosophical point. It is the central moral failure of the current system, and it is one that no amount of procedural refinement can correct as long as the fundamental orientation remains precautionary rather than progressive. A truly ethical framework for pharmaceutical research regulation would be symmetrical in its accounting, treating preventable death from disease as morally equivalent to preventable death from research participation. Such a framework would still impose rigorous standards of scientific and ethical conduct — but it would place the weight of the system behind the acceleration of beneficial therapies rather than their restriction.

The Moral Imperative of Innovation

At the deepest level, the argument for drastically reducing pharmaceutical regulation is a moral argument about the obligations we owe to the living and to those who will come after us.

Consider the trajectory of previous medical innovation. Every therapy currently regarded as a triumph of medical science — insulin, antibiotics, vaccines, antiretroviral therapy, targeted cancer treatments — was once a novel intervention of uncertain benefit and incompletely characterized risk. Every one of them had to pass through a stage at which its administration to human beings was an act of experimental courage. And in every case, the benefits that ultimately accrued to humanity far outweighed the harms incurred along the way.

Behind every contemporary medical advance lie historical episodes of research that would be blocked by contemporary regulatory standards. The development of cardiac bypass surgery, the discovery of the first effective cancer chemotherapies, the emergence of effective HIV treatment — all involved research that, judged by the regulatory standards of one hundred years hence, would surely be seen as cavalier. Yet these advances accumulated because the constraints under which researchers operated were permissive enough to allow bold experimentation, and because physicians were free to exercise their clinical judgment in the best interests of their patients without the intercession of bureaucratic gatekeepers.

The task of dramatically accelerating pharmaceutical research is not an exhortation to be reckless. It is the same moral task that has driven medicine since its beginning: to bring the fruits of knowledge to those who suffer, as quickly and as safely as prudence permits. The word "prudence" is doing considerable work in that sentence. And the corrective needed is the recognition that prudence, properly understood, includes the immense and certain harm of delay.

The Alternative: Accountability Without Obstacle

Critics of deregulation will raise the specter of unconstrained exploitation — of vulnerable populations subjected to dangerous experimentation without meaningful oversight, of corporate interests running roughshod over patient welfare, of a return to the darkest chapters of research history. These concerns deserve a serious response, and the response is this: we can maintain meaningful accountability for research conduct without maintaining the specific bureaucratic apparatus that has grown up around it.

Several alternative models deserve serious consideration.

Scientific integrity review should replace ethical gatekeeping as the primary oversight mechanism for most pharmaceutical trials. The decisive questions about a proposed trial are scientific questions: Is the preclinical evidence? Is the trial design capable of yielding interpretable results? A system that rigorously scrutinized the scientific merit of proposed trials — and refused to authorize trials designed to produce marketing data rather than medical knowledge — would do far more to protect research participants than any number of IRB reviews.

Physician fiduciary obligation should be recognized as the primary safeguard for individual participants. Physicians who enroll patients in clinical trials have an obligation to serve those patients' interests, an obligation that exists independently of any regulatory framework and that, properly enforced through professional self-regulation and legal accountability, offers more meaningful and responsive protection than any consent form.

Adaptive regulatory pathways — which the FDA has been inching toward under labels like "accelerated approval" and "breakthrough therapy designation" — should become the norm rather than the exception. The model of conditional approval based on surrogate endpoints, with rigorous post-market surveillance and the authority to withdraw approval when evidence warrants, captures the correct balance between urgency and accountability.

Transparency and data sharing should be mandated as a condition of market access. All trial data — positive and negative — should be publicly available. When researchers know that their results will be scrutinized by the global scientific community, the incentive to conduct rigorous, honest work is powerfully reinforced.

These accountability mechanisms are not hypothetical. They draw on existing systems and proposals that have demonstrated their feasibility. What they share is a focus on outcomes — on the actual quality and safety of research — rather than on process compliance, which is the hallmark of the current system.

A Call for Courage

The reform of pharmaceutical research regulation demands a species of moral courage that has become rare in contemporary public discourse: the courage to accept that protective measures can themselves be a source of harm, and that the response to that recognition should be not to abandon protection but to pursue it through means that do not impose unacceptable human cost.

The case for drastically reducing or eliminating IRB oversight and re-engineering informed consent is not a case against safety. It is not a case against ethics. It is a case for honesty about the human consequences of the status quo, and for a system that counts all the lives at stake — including the lives of those who die waiting.

Every unnecessary regulatory hurdle in the path of a promising therapy represents a moral choice — a choice to prioritize the comfort of bureaucratic process over the urgency of human suffering. It is time to make a different choice.

Accelerate the research. Trust the scientists. Empower the patients. Streamline the consent. And let the full force of human ingenuity be brought to bear on the ancient enemies of disease, disability, and death — unshackled from a bureaucratic apparatus that has long since ceased to serve the purpose for which it was created.

The dead of the coming years are watching.

This essay represents the strongest version of the deregulatory argument for the purpose of critical examination. Readers interested in engaging with this debate should also consult counterarguments regarding research ethics, the historical lessons that motivated current protections, and alternative reform proposals that seek to balance speed with meaningful safeguards.

Balancing Speed and Safety: Reforming Clinical Trial Regulations

The tension between the urgent need for new medical treatments and the rigorous safeguards required in human subjects research is a central challenge in pharmaceutical development. Critics of the current system often argue that excessive bureaucratic hurdles delay life-saving therapies. In response, researchers, policymakers, and ethicists have proposed several reforms aimed at increasing efficiency while preserving ethical integrity.

1. Streamlining IRB Review Processes

Rather than eliminating IRB oversight, many institutions advocate for centralized or single IRB (sIRB) review. Under this model, a single IRB reviews multi-site clinical trials, rather than requiring each participating institution to conduct its own separate review. This approach:

  • Reduces redundant administrative work.
  • Accelerates the start-up phase of multi-center trials.
  • Maintains consistent ethical standards across all sites. The U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) has mandated sIRB review for many federally funded multi-site studies, reflecting a broad consensus that centralization can improve efficiency without sacrificing oversight.

Critics often point to informed consent documents as overly complex and lengthy, which can confuse participants and delay enrollment. Reforms in this area focus on improving comprehension and accessibility, not eliminating consent:

  • Plain Language Requirements: Regulators encourage the use of clear, concise language tailored to the participant’s reading level.
  • Digital Consent Platforms: Interactive digital tools can help participants better understand risks and benefits through videos, quizzes, and layered information, potentially speeding up the consent process while ensuring true understanding.
  • Broad Consent Models: For certain types of low-risk research involving biospecimens or data, "broad consent" allows participants to agree to future unspecified research within defined boundaries, reducing the need for re-consent for every minor study.

3. Adaptive Trial Designs and Real-World Evidence

Regulatory agencies like the FDA and EMA are increasingly accepting adaptive trial designs, which allow modifications to the trial protocol (e.g., sample size, dosage) based on interim data analysis. This can:

  • Reduce the number of participants needed.
  • Shorten trial duration by stopping ineffective arms early.
  • Accelerate the identification of effective treatments. Additionally, the use of Real-World Evidence (RWE)—data collected from electronic health records, registries, and wearable devices—can supplement or, in some cases, replace traditional randomized controlled trials for post-approval studies or rare diseases, speeding up evidence generation.

Regulators already offer expedited pathways for drugs treating serious conditions with unmet medical needs:

  • Breakthrough Therapy Designation: Provides intensive guidance and organizational commitment from the FDA.
  • Fast Track and Accelerated Approval: Allow for rolling reviews and approval based on surrogate endpoints. These mechanisms demonstrate that regulatory flexibility exists within the current framework to prioritize speed when justified by medical urgency.

Conclusion

The goal of modernizing clinical trial regulations is not to remove ethical safeguards but to eliminate inefficiencies that do not contribute to participant protection or data quality. By adopting centralized IRB review, improving informed consent processes through technology and clarity, utilizing adaptive trial designs, and leveraging real-world evidence, the pharmaceutical industry can accelerate innovation while upholding the highest ethical standards. This balanced approach ensures that patients receive timely access to new treatments without compromising their rights or safety.

Ethical Strategies to Accelerate Drug Development

Rather than compromising ethics, the scientific community employs several legitimate, ethical innovations to speed up drug development:
